mainTopic: Intent and ownership in the laws of an ox that kills: כופר, מיתה, injuries, and the ox's status before and after its verdict
overview: This amud first finishes the מחלוקת between רב and שמואל about an ox that kills without meaning to. The גמרא defends שמואל's case of an ox that pushes over a wall: it is not indirect damage like צרורות, because the wall gave way while the ox was still pushing it. Next, a ברייתא lists four outcomes. It shows that a מועד ox that kills שלא בכוונה is not put to death, but its owner still pays כופר, which supports שמואל and refutes רב. The ברייתא adds a מחלוקת about injuries done without intent. רבי יהודה learns from כופר and makes the owner pay, while רבי שמעון learns from the ox's death penalty and exempts him. The גמרא then shows that our משנה does not follow רבי שמעון, who exempts an ox that aimed at one person and killed another. It traces his view to 'וְאָרַב לוֹ', and explains that the רבנן use that פסוק for someone who throws a stone into a group, a case decided by the rule of קבוע. A new משנה lists unusual oxen that are stoned. רבי יהודה exempts ownerless oxen, even ones that lose their owner after goring, because the owner must exist at the death, the trial and the verdict. A final משנה teaches what happens when the owner consecrates or slaughters the ox before and after the verdict, and that whoever is holding the ox takes the owner's place. A ברייתא about selling the ox before its verdict begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Isn't the falling wall just indirect damage?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל's case. If the wall fell and killed the person, that looks like צרורות (indirect damage), and indirect damage should not bring כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still, this is a case of pebbles!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the case used for שמואל, where an ox pushes a wall and the wall falls on a person. It says this is like צרורות, damage that comes indirectly from the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: צרורות are pebbles kicked up by an animal's feet. That damage is treated as indirect, not the ox's own body doing the act. If the wall falling is the same kind of indirect damage, the owner should not owe כופר, and שמואל's case would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Pebbles kicked up by an animal; the classic example of indirect damage

phrases.english: But still, it is a case of pebbles!
phrases.notes: The ox didn't touch the person; the wall did. So it's indirect, like pebbles kicked up from under a walking animal's feet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of שמואל's wall case from before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of the ox and the wall, used to show an unintentional killing that brings כופר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A wall falling on someone is indirect damage like צרורות, and indirect damage does not bring כופר.

steps.title: The wall gave way gradually while the ox pushed
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא answers: the wall gave way little by little while the ox was still pushing, so the killing counts as the ox's direct act.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, son of רב כהנא, said: it is a case where the wall kept giving way, bit by bit, while the ox pushed it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי answers the challenge. He explains that the wall was collapsing gradually under the ox's ongoing pressure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In צרורות, the force leaves the animal and does damage on its own. Here the ox is still pressing on the wall the whole time it falls, so the ox is still directly involved. That makes it the ox's own act and not indirect damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Little by little, step after step (while still attached to the force)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana, said:
Where it gave way little by little.
phrases.notes: "It" is the wall. It kept falling while the ox was still pushing, so the ox never let go of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the צרורות challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wall fell after the ox's push, so it is separate, indirect damage like צרורות.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wall fell gradually under the ox's continuing pressure, so it counts as the ox's direct act and can bring כופר.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל: four combinations of death and ransom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports שמואל and refutes רב. It lists four possibilities: מיתה and כופר, only כופר, only מיתה, or neither.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with שמואל and refutes רב: sometimes the ox is killed and the owner pays ransom; sometimes the owner pays ransom but the ox is not killed; sometimes the ox is killed but the owner pays no ransom; and sometimes neither happens.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא announces a ברייתא that backs שמואל and is a תיובתא against רב. The ברייתא opens by listing four possible outcomes, which it will explain in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two punishments are separate. מיתה falls on the ox, and כופר falls on the owner. The ברייתא shows they do not always come together, which is what makes room for a case of כופר without מיתה. That case will turn out to be the proof for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Death: here, the ox being put to death
Ransom the owner pays when his ox kills a person

phrases.english: It was taught in accordance with Shmuel,
and it is a refutation of Rav:
There is one liable to death and to ransom,
phrases.notes: Death is for the ox and ransom is for the owner. Keep these two apart all the way through.

phrases.english: and there is one liable to ransom but exempt from death,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ חַיָּיב בְּמִיתָה וּפָטוּר מִן הַכּוֹפֶר,
phrases.english: and there is one liable to death but exempt from ransom,
and there is one exempt from this and from that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending שמואל's case, the גמרא brings outside support for שמואל.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's view that an ox killing שלא בכוונה still brings כופר
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing the four combinations of מיתה and כופר
steps.whyThisMatters: A תיובתא against an אמורא from a ברייתא is very strong. Here it effectively decides the מחלוקת against רב.

steps.title: The four cases explained: מועד or תם, intending or not
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains its four cases. A מועד that kills בכוונה brings both. A מועד that kills שלא בכוונה brings כופר only. A תם that kills בכוונה brings מיתה only. A תם that kills שלא בכוונה brings neither. The second case proves שמואל right.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? A forewarned ox that killed intentionally is killed, and the owner pays ransom. A forewarned ox that killed unintentionally: the owner pays ransom, but the ox is not killed. An innocuous ox that killed intentionally is killed, but the owner pays no ransom. An innocuous ox that killed unintentionally: neither one.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks itself "how so?" and fills in the four outcomes. It does this with two factors: whether the ox is מועד or תם, and whether it killed בכוונה or not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rules are at work. מיתה depends on intent, so only an ox that killed בכוונה is killed. כופר depends on the ox being מועד. So a מועד that killed שלא בכוונה owes כופר even though the ox is not killed, which is exactly שמואל's view against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: A forewarned ox, with a known history of goring
An innocuous ox, with no record of goring

steps.whatToRemember: מיתה follows intent (בכוונה). כופר follows being מועד. So a מועד that kills שלא בכוונה is חייב in כופר but פטור from מיתה, which supports שמואל and refutes רב.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up who gets what. מיתה is a punishment on the ox itself, and כופר is a payment by the owner. One can apply without the other.

phrases.english: How so?
A forewarned ox that killed intentionally is liable to death and to ransom.
A forewarned ox that killed unintentionally:
liable to ransom but exempt from death.
An innocuous ox that killed intentionally:
liable to death but exempt from ransom.
An innocuous ox that killed unintentionally:
exempt from this and from that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the four categories listed in step 3 and contains the actual proof.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's view that a מועד killing שלא בכוונה brings כופר
steps.raayaSupportSource: The line in the ברייתא: מועד שלא בכוונה, חייב בכופר ופטור ממיתה
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule. כופר depends on the ox being מועד, not on its intent.

steps.title: Unintentional injuries: רבי יהודה obligates, רבי שמעון exempts
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that when an ox causes injuries (not death) without intending to, רבי יהודה holds the owner liable and רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for injuries caused unintentionally, רבי יהודה holds the owner liable, and רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves from killing to ordinary damages that the ox causes without intending to. It records a מחלוקת between two תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the ברייתא dealt with death and כופר. Now it asks about regular payment for damage done שלא בכוונה. רבי יהודה says the owner pays and רבי שמעון says he does not, which opens a new question the גמרא can explore next.

phrases.english: And damages caused unintentionally:
Rabbi Yehuda holds liable,
and Rabbi Shimon exempts.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַנְּזָקִין שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מְחַיֵּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The ברייתא continues past the four killing cases to a related question about unintentional injuries.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For damages an ox causes שלא בכוונה, רבי יהודה obligates the owner and רבי שמעון exempts him.

steps.title: What is רבי יהודה's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what source or logic stands behind רבי יהודה's view that the owner pays for injuries the ox caused without meaning to.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה holds the owner liable. This question sets up an explanation of both sides of the מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 only told us the two opinions. Now the גמרא wants the source behind them, starting with רבי יהודה, who holds the owner liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Without intending to (the ox did not aim at this person)

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?
phrases.notes: This goes back to Step 5, where רבי יהודה made the owner pay for injuries the ox caused without meaning to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רבי יהודה's view in the ברייתא's last statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for רבי יהודה's ruling that an owner is liable for unintended injuries.

steps.title: רבי יהודה learns from כופר
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה compares injuries to כופר. Just as כופר is paid even when the ox killed without meaning to, damages for injuries are paid even when the ox injured without meaning to.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from כופר. Just as with כופר the owner is liable even when it was unintended, so too with injuries he is liable even when it was unintended.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה learns the law of injuries from the law of כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 showed that a מועד ox that kills without meaning to still brings כופר. רבי יהודה applies the same rule to injuries: lack of intent does not exempt the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: The ransom payment an owner makes when his מועד ox kills a person
Damages, here injuries the ox causes

phrases.english: He learns it from its ransom (כופר);
just as with its ransom, he is liable even when it was unintended,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַנְּזָקִין נָמֵי – שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: so too with injuries, he is liable even when it was unintended.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה compares injuries to כופר, which is paid even without intent.

steps.title: רבי שמעון learns from the ox being put to death
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון compares injuries to the death penalty of the ox. The ox is not killed when it killed without meaning to, so the owner does not pay for injuries it caused without meaning to.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שמעון learns from the ox's being killed. Just as its being killed does not apply when it was unintended, so too with injuries there is an exemption when it was unintended.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי שמעון's source: the law that an ox is put to death only when it killed on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 showed that an ox that kills without meaning to is not put to death. רבי שמעון applies the same rule to injuries: without intent, there is no liability.

keyTerms.meaning: The killing of the ox (the death penalty for an ox that killed a person)

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides learn from the same case, an ox that kills a person. They just pick different laws within that case: רבי יהודה picks the כופר payment and רבי שמעון picks the ox's death penalty.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shimon learns from the killing of the ox,
just as with its being killed, when it was unintended it is exempt,
so too with injuries, when it was unintended he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the מחלוקת, parallel to רבי יהודה's source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי שמעון compares injuries to the ox's death penalty, which needs intent.

steps.title: Why doesn't רבי יהודה learn from the ox's death?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה: there are two possible sources, so why does he choose כופר and not the ox's death penalty?
steps.simpleTranslation: And let רבי יהודה also learn from the ox's being killed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה ignores רבי שמעון's source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both laws come from the same case of an ox that kills. Without a reason to prefer one, רבי יהודה's choice of כופר looks random.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda too, let him learn from its being killed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהודה's choice of source in Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's choice to learn from כופר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is another available source, the ox's death penalty, that leads to an exemption. Why not use it?

steps.title: Payment is learned from payment
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה holds that a payment law, like damages for injury, should be learned from another payment law, like כופר, and not from a death penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn payments from payments, and we do not learn payments from death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה picks כופר because it is a payment, just like damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damages for injuries are money. כופר is money too, while the ox's death penalty is a different kind of law. So כופר is the closer comparison.

keyTerms.meaning: We judge or learn (one law from another)
Death (here, the ox being put to death)

phrases.english: We learn payments from payments,
phrases.notes: He means damages for injury can be learned from כופר, since both are money payments.

phrases.english: and we do not learn payments from death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the two possible sources are not equally similar.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources are equally good, so רבי יהודה's choice looks random.
steps.terutzMaskana: כופר is a payment like damages, so it is the better source.

steps.title: Why doesn't רבי שמעון learn from כופר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the question around: given רבי יהודה's argument that payment should be learned from payment, why does רבי שמעון not learn from כופר?
steps.simpleTranslation: And let רבי שמעון also learn from כופר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges רבי שמעון's choice of source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 made a strong case that כופר is the more similar source because it is a payment. So רבי שמעון seems to need a reason to reject it.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shimon too, let him learn from its ransom (כופר)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors Step 9, now aimed at רבי שמעון.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון's choice to learn from the ox's death penalty.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: כופר is a payment like damages, so it seems the better source.

steps.title: The ox's liability is learned from the ox's liability
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון holds that damages are a liability tied to the ox, like its death penalty. כופר is a liability on the owner, so it is not a good comparison.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn the ox's liability from the ox's liability. That leaves out כופר, which is a liability of the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי שמעון compares based on whose liability it is, not on whether it is money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, the key feature is that both damages and the death penalty come from the ox's own act. כופר is the owner's own obligation, so it is a different kind of law. Each side simply picks a different point of similarity.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה (liable): learns injuries from כופר, because both are payments. רבי שמעון (exempt): learns injuries from the ox's death penalty, because both are liabilities of the ox, while כופר is the owner's liability.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in the גמרא: both sides of a מחלוקת use the same method of learning one law from another. They disagree only about which shared feature matters most.

phrases.english: We learn the liability of the ox from the liability of the ox,
phrases.notes: He means damages and the death penalty both come from what the ox itself did.

phrases.english: which leaves out the ransom (כופר), which is a liability of the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 11 and completes the explanation of both opinions.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a different shared feature that makes the death penalty the better source.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כופר is the better source because it is a payment.
steps.terutzMaskana: What matters is whose liability it is, and כופר belongs to the owner, not the ox.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה and learning from its wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's exemption and infers that an ox meaning to kill one person but killing another is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: if the ox meant to kill an animal and killed a person, it is exempt. So if it meant to kill this person and killed that person, it is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the משנה and drawing an inference from its wording. This sets up the next step, which shows who the משנה agrees with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only exempts cases where the ox meant to kill a different kind of victim, like an animal. The גמרא reads this precisely: if the ox meant to kill one person and killed a different person, both are people, so the ox would be stoned.

phrases.english: If it intended to kill the animal
and it killed the person, etc., it is exempt.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the rest of the משנה's list, like meaning to kill someone the ox would not be stoned for and killing someone else.

phrases.english: This implies: if it intended to kill this person
and it killed that person, it is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא נִתְכַּוֵּין לַהֲרוֹג אֶת זֶה, וְהָרַג אֶת זֶה – חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the injury discussion and opens a new topic from the משנה about an ox that kills.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From the wording of the משנה, an ox that meant to kill one person and killed another person is liable.

steps.title: The משנה does not follow רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: Because of that inference, the משנה cannot follow רבי שמעון, who exempts the ox even when it meant to kill one person and killed another.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה is not like רבי שמעון. A ברייתא teaches: רבי שמעון says that even if it meant to kill this person and killed that person, it is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that the משנה goes against רבי שמעון's view, and it brings a ברייתא to show what רבי שמעון holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The inference from the last step makes the ox liable when it switches from one person to another. רבי שמעון exempts that case, so the משנה must follow the רבנן. This sets up the question of where רבי שמעון gets his view.

keyTerms.meaning: which is not in line with

steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון does not mean the ox is innocent in general. He means the death penalty applies only when the ox killed the exact victim it was aiming at.

phrases.english: Our mishna is not in line with Rabbi Shimon.
As it is taught: Rabbi Shimon says:
Even if it intended to kill this one
and it killed that one, it is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the inference from step 13 to decide whose view the משנה follows.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה follows the רבנן, not רבי שמעון, who exempts an ox that killed someone other than its target.

steps.title: What is רבי שמעון's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of רבי שמעון's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי שמעון's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי שמעון learns his view. This sets up the answer from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a plain request for a source, not an attack on רבי שמעון. The גמרא wants to know why aiming at a different person should exempt the ox.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the view quoted in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for רבי שמעון's exemption.

steps.title: The ox's death is like the owner's death
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק puts the ox's stoning next to the owner's death penalty. Just as a person is liable only if he meant to kill that victim, so is the ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'The ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.' The ox's death is like the owner's death. A person is liable only if he meant to kill that victim, and the same is true for the ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק that links the ox's death penalty to a person's death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the פסוק mentions the ox and the owner together, רבי שמעון applies the same rules to both. A murderer is liable only if he aimed at the person he killed, so the ox is too. This rests on the rule for the owner, which the גמרא asks about next.

keyTerms.meaning: owner; here, a person who kills
only when he aims at him

phrases.english: Because the verse says:
"The ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death"
like the death of the owner, so is the death of the ox;
just as the owner is liable only when he aims at him,
phrases.notes: 'Owner' here stands for any person who kills: a person is put to death only if he aimed at the one he killed.

phrases.aramaic: אַף שׁוֹר נָמֵי – עַד דְּמִיכַּוֵּין לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: so too the ox, only when it aims at him.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר קְרָא: הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק compares the ox's death to the owner's death, so the ox, like a person, is liable only when it aimed at the victim.

steps.title: Where do we learn the rule for the owner himself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that a person is liable only if he meant to kill that very victim.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the owner himself, where do we learn this?
steps.whatsHappening: The ox's rule depends on the owner's rule, so the גמרא now asks for the source of the owner's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison in step 16 only works if we already know that a human killer must aim at his actual victim. The גמרא wants a פסוק for that base rule.

phrases.english: And the owner himself, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind the comparison used in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that a human killer is liable only if he intended to kill that specific victim.

steps.title: From the words 'And he lay in wait for him'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' shows that a killer is liable only when he aimed at the person he killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And he lay in wait for him and rose against him.' That means he is liable only when he aimed at him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי שמעון's source for the owner's rule: the word 'for him' in the פסוק about a murderer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון reads 'לוֹ' to mean that the killer must be aiming at this exact person. If he aimed at someone else and killed this one, he is not put to death, and through step 16 neither is the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: and he lay in wait for him

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון: a killer, whether a person or an ox, is put to death only when it killed the exact one it aimed at. The source is 'וְאָרַב לוֹ', carried over to the ox through 'הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת'.

phrases.english: Because the verse says:
"And he lay in wait for him and rose against him"
only when he aims at him.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר קְרָא: וְאָרַב לוֹ וְקָם עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' teaches that a killer is liable only when he intended to kill that very person.

steps.title: How do the רבנן use 'וְאָרַב לוֹ'?
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not learn רבי שמעון's rule from 'וְאָרַב לוֹ', so the גמרא asks what they learn from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, what do they do with this 'and he lay in wait for him'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the רבנן learn from the same words, since they do not use them like רבי שמעון does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן hold that a killer who aimed at one person and killed another is liable. Still, every word of the פסוק should teach something, so they must use 'לוֹ' for some other rule.

keyTerms.meaning: what do they do with it, meaning what do they learn from it

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, this "and he lay in wait for him"
what do they do with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, הַאי וְאָרַב לוֹ מַאי עָבְדִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from רבי שמעון's reading of the פסוק to the רבנן's use of it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What rule the רבנן learn from 'וְאָרַב לוֹ'.

steps.title: It exempts throwing a stone into a mixed group
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי says the פסוק exempts someone who throws a stone into a group of people.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי says: this comes to exclude someone who throws a stone into a group.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן use 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' for a different case: a stone thrown into a group without aiming at anyone in particular.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the רבנן, 'לוֹ' means the killer must be aiming at a person he would be liable for. If he throws into a mixed group, which includes people he would not be put to death for, he is exempt even if the stone kills someone he would be liable for. So the רבנן still learn something from 'לוֹ', just a narrower rule than רבי שמעון.

keyTerms.meaning: one who throws a stone into a group

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides learn from 'וְאָרַב לוֹ'. רבי שמעון: the killer must aim at the exact victim. רבנן: the killer must at least aim at someone he would be liable for, so throwing into a mixed group is exempt.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai says:
to exclude one who throws a stone into a group.
phrases.notes: He means a group that includes people he would not be put to death for, so he was not aiming at one particular person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי: פְּרָט לַזּוֹרֵק אֶבֶן לְגוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן use 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' to exempt someone who throws a stone into a mixed group.

steps.title: Which crowd could the rule be talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the teaching of רבי ינאי's school. If the crowd is mostly gentiles, we follow the majority. If it is half and half, we are lenient anyway. So why would we need a פסוק?
steps.simpleTranslation: What case is this? If there are nine gentiles and one Jew, the thrower is exempt simply because most of the group are gentiles. And if it is half and half, he is exempt because in a doubt about a death penalty we are lenient.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the teaching from Step 20 (someone who throws a stone into a group is exempt). It shows that in the obvious cases he would be exempt even without a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסוק should teach something we could not figure out alone. A mostly gentile group is covered by the rule of רוב. A half-and-half group is covered by ספק נפשות להקל. So the גמרא is pushing to find a case where the פסוק is actually needed.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
Derive it from somewhere else; you don't need this source
Majority; we follow what most of the group is
When there is a doubt about a death penalty, we rule leniently

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If we say that there are nine gentiles
and one Jew among them,
derive the exemption from the fact that most of them are gentiles;
and even if it is half and half,
a doubt about a death penalty is ruled leniently!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the teaching of רבי ינאי's school by asking which case would need it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' is needed to exempt someone who throws a stone into a group.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In every obvious version of the case, the exemption already follows from רוב or from ספק נפשות להקל, so the פסוק looks unnecessary.

steps.title: Nine Jews and one gentile: the rule of קבוע
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is needed when most of the group are Jews. Because the gentile is standing in a fixed group, the case is not judged by majority. It counts as a 50/50 doubt, so the thrower is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the פסוק is needed where there are nine Jews and one gentile. Most of them are Jews, but one gentile is among them, so the case is 'קבוע'. Anything קבוע is treated like half and half, and in a doubt about a death penalty we are lenient.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is needed for a group that is mostly Jews with one gentile. Even there, the thrower is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think majority rules, so he should be treated as having thrown at Jews. But when the people stand together in place, the rule of קבוע says we don't follow the majority; it counts as an even 50/50 doubt. Once it is a doubt, ספק נפשות להקל exempts him. 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' teaches this.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed for this specific case
Fixed in place; the items are still in their set location, not separated from the group
It is treated like an even, half-and-half doubt

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן learn from 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' that someone who throws a stone into a group of nine Jews and one gentile is exempt. The gentile is קבוע, which makes it a 50/50 doubt, and in a doubt about a death penalty we are lenient.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think majority always decides. When the group is קבוע (fixed in place), we ignore the majority and treat it as an exact 50/50 doubt.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where there are nine Jews and one gentile.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּרוּבָּא יִשְׂרְאֵלִים נִינְהוּ;
phrases.english: For even though most of them are Jews,
since there is one gentile among them,
it counts as 'fixed,'
phrases.notes: The people are all standing together in their places, not separated from the group.

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל קָבוּעַ כְּמֶחֱצָה עַל מֶחֱצָה דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: and anything fixed is treated like half and half,
and a doubt about a death penalty is ruled leniently.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִיכָּא תִּשְׁעָה יִשְׂרְאֵלִים וְאֶחָד גּוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by pointing to a case where the פסוק is really needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the פסוק, we would follow the majority of Jews and make the thrower liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because of קבוע the case counts as a 50/50 doubt, so the thrower is exempt; that is what 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' teaches.

steps.title: Oxen with unusual owners or no owner: are they stoned?
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה lists six kinds of oxen that are stoned for killing a person. רבי יהודה exempts the three that have no owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox belonging to a woman, an ox belonging to orphans, an ox in the care of a guardian, a desert ox, a הקדש ox, and the ox of a convert who died without heirs are all put to death. רבי יהודה says the desert ox, the הקדש ox, and the dead convert's ox are exempt from death, because they have no owners.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists unusual oxen and rules that they are stoned if they kill a person, with רבי יהודה disagreeing about the ownerless ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first group (woman, orphans, guardian) has owners, just unusual ones. The second group (desert ox, הקדש, a convert with no heirs) has no private owner at all. The תנא קמא stones all of them, but רבי יהודה says stoning applies only to an ox that has an owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Guardian or steward who manages property for others, such as orphans
Desert ox; a wild ox that belongs to no one
Property dedicated to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: MISHNA
An ox belonging to a woman, and an ox belonging to orphans,
an ox in the care of a guardian, a desert ox,
a consecrated ox,

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר הַגֵּר שֶׁמֵּת וְאֵין לוֹ יוֹרְשִׁין –
phrases.english: an ox of a convert who died and has no heirs,
these are all liable to death.
Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, שׁוֹר הַהֶקְדֵּשׁ, שׁוֹר הַגֵּר שֶׁמֵּת –
phrases.english: A desert ox, a consecrated ox, and the ox of a convert who died
are exempt from death,
since they have no owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All six types of oxen are stoned for killing a person; רבי יהודה exempts the three ownerless ones.

steps.title: The source: the word 'ox' appears seven times
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that the Torah repeats 'שׁוֹר' seven times in order to include the six special oxen of the משנה. רבי יהודה again exempts the ownerless ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'Ox,' 'ox' appears seven times, to include an ox of a woman, of orphans, of a guardian, a desert ox, a הקדש ox, and the ox of a convert who died with no heirs. רבי יהודה says the desert ox, the הקדש ox, and the dead convert's ox are exempt from death, since they have no owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives the Torah source for the משנה's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'שׁוֹר' appears seven times in the passage. One is for the basic case, so the other six each include one of the six unusual oxen. רבי יהודה still holds that an ox with no owner is not stoned.

keyTerms.meaning: To include; the extra word adds more cases

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the Torah's repeated words become the source for the משנה's list of cases.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Sages taught:
'Ox,' 'ox,' seven times,
phrases.notes: שמות 21:28–32. One mention is the basic case, which leaves six extras for the six oxen listed.

phrases.english: to include an ox belonging to a woman,
an ox belonging to orphans, an ox in the care of a guardian,
a desert ox, a consecrated ox,

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר הַגֵּר שֶׁמֵּת וְאֵין לוֹ יוֹרְשִׁין.
phrases.english: and an ox of a convert who died and has no heirs.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
A desert ox, a consecrated ox,

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר הַגֵּר שֶׁמֵּת וְאֵין לוֹ יוֹרְשִׁין –
phrases.english: and an ox of a convert who died and has no heirs
are exempt from death,
since they have no owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the Torah source for the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seven mentions of 'שׁוֹר' include the six special oxen in the death penalty; רבי יהודה exempts the ownerless ones.

steps.title: רב הונא: רבי יהודה exempts even if ownership was dropped after the goring
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says רבי יהודה exempts an ox even when it gored while owned and only later was made הקדש or הפקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא says: רבי יהודה would exempt the ox even if it gored and afterward the owner consecrated it, or it gored and afterward he made it ownerless.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא expands רבי יהודה's view from the previous steps. It is not only an ox that was ownerless when it killed; even one that loses its owner later is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה and ברייתא, רבי יהודה exempted the three ownerless oxen. רב הונא says the timing is wider than we might think. If the ox has no owner by the time of the trial, רבי יהודה exempts it, even though it had an owner when it killed.

keyTerms.meaning: He consecrated it, giving it to the Temple
He gave up ownership, making it ownerless

phrases.english: Rav Huna says:
Rabbi Yehuda would exempt
even if it gored and afterward he consecrated it,
or it gored and afterward he made it ownerless.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: פּוֹטֵר הָיָה רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands רבי יהודה's exemption from steps 23-24 to cases where ownership is lost after the killing
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, an ox that killed while owned is exempt if the owner later made it הקדש or הפקר.

steps.title: Where does רב הונא learn this from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for רב הונא's source.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רב הונא knows this. It is setting up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only listed ownerless oxen and never mentioned an ox that lost its owner later. So the גמרא wants to see what text supports רב הונא's wider reading.

keyTerms.meaning: From where? What is the source?

phrases.english: From where do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רב הונא's statement
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The textual basis for saying רבי יהודה exempts even when ownership was lost after the goring

steps.title: Proof from the extra case of the convert's ox
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists both a desert ox and a dead convert's ox. Both are simply ownerless, so the second case must teach that ownership lost after the goring also exempts.
steps.simpleTranslation: From the fact that it teaches two cases: a desert ox, and the ox of a convert who died and has no heirs. What is the ox of a convert who died? Since he has no heirs, it is an ownerless ox. If so, it is the same as the desert ox! Rather, doesn't it teach us that even if it gored and afterward he consecrated it, or gored and afterward he made it ownerless, it is exempt? Conclude from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that two cases in רבי יהודה's list seem to say the same thing. It explains that the extra case must teach רב הונא's point, and it accepts the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A desert ox and a dead convert's ox with no heirs are both just ownerless. Listing both would be pointless unless the convert's case is different. The difference is that the convert was alive when the ox gored and died afterward. That teaches that losing the owner after the goring is enough to exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: A desert ox, one with no owner
A convert. If he dies with no heirs, his property becomes ownerless.
This is what it teaches us
Conclude from it, so the proof stands

phrases.english: From the fact that it teaches two cases:
a desert ox,

phrases.aramaic: וְשׁוֹר הַגֵּר שֶׁמֵּת וְאֵין לוֹ יוֹרְשִׁין.
phrases.english: and the ox of a convert who died and has no heirs.
The ox of a convert who died, what is it?
Since he has no heirs,
it is an ownerless ox;
so that is the same as a desert ox,

phrases.aramaic: הַיְינוּ שׁוֹר הַגֵּר שֶׁמֵּת וְאֵין לוֹ יוֹרְשִׁין!
phrases.english: it is the same as the ox of a convert who died and has no heirs!

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן –
phrases.english: Rather, doesn't it teach us this:
that even if it gored and afterward he consecrated it,
or it gored and afterward he made it ownerless, it is exempt?
Conclude from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26 with a proof from the wording of the ברייתא
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's claim that רבי יהודה exempts even when ownership was lost after the goring
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra case in the ברייתא of the dead convert's ox, which would otherwise repeat the desert ox

steps.title: A ברייתא says it openly and gives the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא states that רבי יהודה exempts even when the ox was made הקדש or הפקר after goring. The source is the פסוק, read as requiring the same owner at the death and at the trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way: Moreover, רבי יהודה said: even if it gored and afterward he consecrated it, or gored and afterward he made it ownerless, it is exempt. As it says: 'and warning has been given to its owner... and it killed, etc.' This means the ox is exempt unless its status at the death and at the trial is the same.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says רב הונא's point in plain words. It also gives the פסוק behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא joins two parts of the פסוק. 'Warning has been given to its owner' refers to the owner standing in court. 'And it killed' refers to the death. Joining them teaches that the ox needs an owner both at the death and at the trial. If ownership is gone by the trial, the ox is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: And warning has been given to its owner
Standing in court, the time of the trial

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵר עַל כֵּן אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Moreover, Rabbi Yehuda said:
even if it gored and afterward he consecrated it,
or it gored and afterward he made it ownerless, it is exempt,
as it says: 'and warning has been given to its owner'
'and it killed, etc.'
unless the death and the standing in court
are the same, as one.
phrases.notes: He means the ox must have an owner both when it kills and when the case comes to court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds open support from a ברייתא to the proof of step 27
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's statement about רבי יהודה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבי יהודה, with the פסוק 'וְהוּעַד בִּבְעָלָיו... וְהֵמִית'

steps.title: What about the verdict?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the ברייתא leaves out the verdict, even though the פסוק 'הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל' refers to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And don't we need the verdict too? But 'the ox shall be stoned' is the verdict!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא. It only mentioned two points in time, but the פסוק points to a third one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same פסוק goes on to say 'the ox shall be stoned,' which is the court's final verdict. So the ox should need an owner at the verdict as well. Why did the ברייתא list only the death and the trial?

keyTerms.meaning: The final verdict of the court

phrases.english: And don't we need the verdict too?
But 'the ox shall be stoned' is the verdict!
phrases.notes: These words come in the same פסוק, שמות 21:29.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא brought in step 28
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that only the death and the trial must match
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק also says 'הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל', which is the verdict, so the verdict should be a required point too

steps.title: Correct the wording: death, trial, and verdict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא's wording. The ox's status must be the same at the death, the trial, and the verdict.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: unless the death, and the standing in court, and the verdict are the same, as one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing the wording of the ברייתא so it includes the verdict too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule does not change direction; it is made complete. The ox needs an owner at all three points: when it kills, when the case is brought to court, and when the verdict is given. If ownership is missing at any of them, רבי יהודה exempts the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say it this way (the גמרא corrects the wording)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהודה, an ox is stoned only if it has an owner at all three points: the killing, the trial, and the verdict. Losing ownership afterward through הקדש, הפקר, or the owner's death with no heirs exempts it.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
unless the death, and the standing in court,
and the verdict are the same, as one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 29 by correcting the ברייתא's wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the death and the trial must match
steps.terutzMaskana: The death, the trial, and the verdict must all match

steps.title: Consecrating or slaughtering an ox before and after its verdict
steps.stepSummary: After the death verdict, הקדש does not take effect on the ox and its meat is forbidden even if slaughtered. Before the verdict, the ox becomes הקדש and slaughtered meat is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: An ox already being taken out to be stoned cannot be consecrated by its owner, and if he slaughters it, its meat is forbidden. But if the owner consecrated it before its verdict was final, it is consecrated, and if he slaughtered it then, its meat is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that the moment of the final verdict decides whether the owner can still consecrate the ox or eat it after slaughter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the verdict is final, the ox is already condemned and forbidden, so the owner has nothing left to give to הקדש and slaughter does not permit it. Before the verdict, the ox is still a normal animal, so הקדש and slaughter work as usual. This fits Step 30, where the verdict was one of the key moments that decides the ox's status.

keyTerms.meaning: Being taken out to be stoned, meaning after the verdict
He consecrated it, giving it to the Temple
Its verdict was finished, meaning final
Its meat is forbidden or permitted

steps.confusionAlert: Slaughtering the ox does not rescue it after the verdict. Once the verdict is final, the meat stays forbidden no matter how the ox dies.
steps.whyThisMatters: The finished verdict is a turning point that permanently changes the ox's status. This links straight back to Step 30, which stressed the verdict as a key moment.

phrases.english: MISHNA: An ox that is going out to be stoned,
and its owner consecrated it – it is not consecrated.
If he slaughtered it – its meat is forbidden.
But if, before its verdict was finished,
its owner consecrated it – it is consecrated.
And if he slaughtered it – its meat is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה. It continues the theme of Step 30, that the verdict is a key moment for the ox's status.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the final verdict, הקדש does not take effect and slaughtered meat is forbidden. Before the verdict, הקדש takes effect and slaughtered meat is permitted.

steps.title: Watchmen, borrowers and renters take the owner's place
steps.stepSummary: Whoever holds the ox for the owner, whether a שומר חנם, שואל, נושא שכר or שוכר, takes the owner's responsibility for its damage. They pay in full for a מועד and half for a תם.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the owner handed the ox to an unpaid watchman, a borrower, a paid watchman or a renter, they take the owner's place. If the ox is a מועד, the holder pays full damages. If it is a תם, the holder pays half damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a second rule. When someone else is holding the ox, that person pays for its damage instead of the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All four kinds of holder are treated alike here. Each one steps into the owner's shoes. The amount paid still depends on the ox itself: full damages for a מועד and half damages for a תם.

keyTerms.meaning: They step into the owner's place
An ox with a goring history, or one without

steps.whatToRemember: Whoever holds the ox takes on the owner's liability. A מועד means full damages and a תם means half damages.

phrases.english: If he handed it to an unpaid watchman or to a borrower,
to a paid watchman or to a renter –
they step into the place of the owner;
if it is forewarned – he pays full damages,
and if it is innocuous – he pays half damages.
phrases.notes: "He" here is whoever was holding the ox, not the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second clause of the same משנה, moving from the ox's own status to who pays for its damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any of the four kinds of holder takes the owner's place: full damages for a מועד and half damages for a תם.

steps.title: A ברייתא begins: an ox that killed and was sold before its verdict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts quoting a ברייתא about an ox that killed a person and was sold before its verdict. The amud ends in the middle of the sentence, so the ruling comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The רבנן taught: An ox that killed a person, and before its verdict was finished, its owner sold it...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא that builds on the first rule of the משנה. This line only sets up the case, and its ruling continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה dealt with consecrating and slaughtering before the verdict. The ברייתא now adds a new action: selling the ox before the verdict. What the sale accomplishes has not been said yet.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
An ox that killed a person;
before its verdict was finished – he sold it

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה, adding a sale before the verdict to the actions discussed in Step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup only: an ox that killed was sold before its verdict. The ruling continues on the next amud.
